name: Tomas Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Castle Mead, the Ashby family's place, about six hundred hectares of wheat, beans and oilseed rape, plus a hundred and twenty suckler cows. This time of year it's drilling the last of the winter wheat, feeding the cattle and fixing whatever broke in the autumn. I'm junior, two years in, and I still get the drilling depth wrong sometimes, Mr Ashby pulls up a seed with his fingers and just looks at me. But I'm the one with the AI on my phone checking the weather models and the grain prices before breakfast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use the AI day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everything, honestly. Grain markets, working out spray rates, writing up the cattle records, even drafting a business plan for my own thing. I want to start a contracting business, drone spraying and mapping for farms round here, and the AI's helped me cost it out. My brothers think I'm mad, my mum lights a candle for me at Mass every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to describe five pictures of the future and ask the same questions about each. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a shame, and then get on with it. People who wait for the next big thing never build anything. I'd post something about it, probably a picture of the drone with a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be fine for me, maybe even better. If the big tech doesn't sweep in, there's room for a small bloke with a drone and a good reputation. Less competition from some company with a fleet of robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push ahead with the drone business on weekends. The kit's about six thousand, so I'd put in two thousand of my savings and get a small loan for the rest, and keep my job at Castle Mead for steady money. I'd sign up two or three farms I know through the young farmers to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Keen, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Six thousand is a lot against a few months' savings. What does Ana say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says don't touch the money for the car. She's a vet nurse, so she's seen what happens when farmers overreach. We agreed I can use a third of my savings, not more, and the rest comes from work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mr Ashby mind you running a business on the side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I asked him already. He said as long as his wheat's sprayed first and on time. He's a businessman himself, he gets it.

S0.say: I'd say that's a shame and get on with it, because people who wait for the next big thing never build anything. I'd post a picture of my drone with a joke.
S0.think: It would be fine for me, maybe better, because without big tech sweeping in there's room for a small contractor with a drone and a good name.
S0.do: Starts weekend drone spraying, putting about two thousand of savings and a small loan toward six thousand of kit while keeping his farm job. Signs up two or three farms through the young farmers' club.
S0.quote: If the big tech doesn't sweep in, there's room for a small bloke with a drone and a good reputation.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is already planning a business and treats AI tools as everyday kit. His partner, a vet nurse, acts as a brake on risk, and he respects the limit. His traditional and free-market views show in his faith, his family and his belief in building your own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Right, now the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to be young and willing. The government should keep out of the way and let people build. Cut the red tape on drone licences, for a start, it took me eight months to get mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my best scenario. Farms will need people who can set up and run the new kit, and I'd already be doing it. The risk is the big contractors coming in with fleets, so I'd need to move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time with the contracting within a year, keeping a couple of days at Castle Mead. I'd buy a second drone and an AI weed-mapping system, which is a camera that spots weeds so you only spray where they are, and hire my younger brother Marco. I'd put most of my savings in and borrow the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. A bit nervous about the loan, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put most of your savings in. What does Ana think now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I promised a third. I'd say the world changed. We'd argue about it on the drive to her mum's, and we'd end up at half, probably. She's usually right about the half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Mr Ashby's workers, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Frank on the sprayer, he'd lose that job to me, really. I'd feel bad. I'd offer him work driving the van, because he knows every farm gate in the county.

S1.say: I'd say it's a great time to be young and willing, and the government should cut red tape such as the eight months it took to get a drone licence.
S1.think: This is my best scenario, because farms will need people who can run the new kit and I'd already be doing it. The danger is big contractors arriving with fleets, so I'd need to move fast.
S1.do: Takes his contracting business nearly full-time within a year, buys a second drone and an AI weed-mapping system, and hires his younger brother. Puts about half his savings in and borrows the rest.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, slightly nervous about the loan.
S1.quote: She'd say I promised a third. I'd say the world changed.
S1.fieldNote: Tomas sees steady change as his chance and plans to bring automation to other farms himself. He blames red tape rather than big tech, which fits his free-market outlook. He would hire family first and thought of a job for the older sprayer driver he'd displace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three end at full AGI. What changes is how much time there is. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, but the answer is people helping each other, families and churches and businesses, not everyone sitting on benefits. I'd say keep working, whatever comes. I'd mean it, but I'd be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years kills my business before it starts. If AI can do almost anything and robots can fly drones, the big companies run it all from an office. A small contractor's just in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not buy the second drone, and I'd make what money I could from the first while farms still need people for a year or so. I'd pay off the loan as fast as possible and keep every penny after that. If it fell apart, I'd lean on my family, my parents have a bit of land and we'd farm it together, the old way if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but the excitement's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Farming the family land the old way, what would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Veg, a few pigs, hens, maybe sell at the market on Saturdays. My grandfather fed eight kids off less. It wouldn't be a business plan, it'd be keeping the family fed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not benefits, but would you take government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to everyone, I'd take it, I'm not stupid. But I'd want to be doing something with my hands while I did. Sitting at home would drive me mad.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast for anyone, but the answer is families, churches and businesses helping each other, not everyone on benefits. I'd tell people to keep working whatever comes.
S2.think: Two years kills my business before it starts, because if robots can fly drones, big companies run everything from an office and a small contractor is just in the way.
S2.do: Cancels the second drone, earns what he can from the first while farms still need people, and pays off the loan fast. Leans on his family and farms his parents' land together if things fall apart.
S2.quote: My grandfather fed eight kids off less. It wouldn't be a business plan, it'd be keeping the family fed.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI turns Tomas from builder to protector: pay off the loan, fall back on family land. His public line against benefits softens privately to accepting a payment if everyone gets one. He still needs to work with his hands to feel all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, with five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make some money and get ready, if you're quick. Don't wait for the government to tell you what to do. I'd say that at young farmers and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd go hard for three years and then be careful. Build the business, make what I can while farms are switching, and get out before the robots don't need me. It's like harvest, you work flat out while the weather holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd buy the second drone and the weed mapper, take on Marco, and sign up as many farms as I could. I'd use AI for everything, quotes, routes, invoices, and keep costs low. By year three I'd start paying down debt and putting money into something solid, maybe a field or two of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. I like having a clock to beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a field or two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because land's land. Whatever happens with robots, people need to eat, and owning the ground is better than owning a drone that's out of date in a year. My dad always said, buy land, they're not making any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you'd be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day a farmer tells me his new robot does what I do, for less. That'll come, I just don't know when. I'd want to have the debt gone before then.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to make money and get ready if you're quick, and people shouldn't wait for the government to tell them what to do.
S3.think: I'd go hard for three years while farms are switching, then get careful and get out before robots don't need me, like working flat out at harvest while the weather holds.
S3.do: Expands the drone business in year one with a second drone, a weed mapper and his brother, using AI for quotes and invoices. From year three pays down debt and buys a field or two of land.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, enjoying a clock to beat.
S3.quote: It's like harvest, you work flat out while the weather holds.
S3.fieldNote: Tomas sees five years as a harvest window: make hay, then put it into land. His instinct is to turn temporary gains into something solid his family can hold. He named the exact moment he dreads, a farmer telling him a robot does his job cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who's willing to work. Build something, own something, and look after your family. That's what I'd say, and it's what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not that worried. In ten years I could have a proper business, some land, a family, and I'd be thirty-seven with assets instead of a wage. If the robots do the work, I'd rather own a few of them than be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the contracting business steadily, not too fast, and buy robots and drones as they get cheaper. Ana and I would get married in the next couple of years, like we've talked about, and put money into a small farm when the right one comes up. I'd keep using AI for everything and teach Marco to as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. More excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your worry, if you have one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, really. She cleans at the school, and she's never touched a computer. If her work goes, I'd want to be the son who can look after her. That's half of why I want to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And faith, does it come into how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. I don't think a robot changes what a man's for. You still look after your family, you still go to Mass. The tools change, that's all.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work: build something, own something and look after your family. It's also what I'd do.
S4.think: I'm not that worried, because in ten years I could have a business, some land and a family, and be thirty-seven with assets instead of a wage. I'd rather own a few robots than be replaced by them.
S4.do: Grows the contracting business steadily, buying robots and drones as they get cheaper and teaching his brother to use AI. Marries his partner in the next couple of years and buys a small farm when the right one comes up.
S4.feel: Calm and more excited than worried.
S4.quote: I'd rather own a few of them than be replaced by them.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Tomas is confident and plans to own the change. His motive turns out to be family: he wants to be able to look after his mother, a school cleaner. His faith gives him a fixed point that technology doesn't touch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It'd catch me with a loan and a business that's suddenly worthless. What would help is less red tape so small businesses can move fast, and some breathing room on business loans if the bottom falls out. And help for people like my mum, the ones who can't switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith or family much, and that's what holds people up when work goes. I don't think a robot changes what a man's for. Or a woman.

headlineQuote: I don't think a robot changes what a man's for.
portrait: Tomas Reyes is a 27-year-old junior worker at Castle Mead, a large arable and beef farm, where he still gets the drilling depth wrong but checks grain prices with AI before breakfast. He lives with Ana, a vet nurse who keeps his business plans in check, and is building a weekend drone spraying business with a third of his savings. Steady change looks like his best chance, and he'd go nearly full-time and hire his brother. AGI in two years would kill the business before it starts and send him back to family land, but with five or ten years he plans to make money while farms switch and put it into land and robots of his own. His faith and family, especially his mother, sit at the centre of how he sees it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would catch him with a loan and a business that had suddenly lost its value.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape so small businesses can move fast, breathing room on business loans, and support for people like his mother who can't switch.
